overview.title: 📖 Overview: Naming a Limb, and Naming a Nation
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 5a–5b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara first asks how much of an animal becomes consecrated when one names only its leg as a burnt offering, weighing Rabbi Meir's view that only the limb is sacred against Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon's view that the whole animal becomes holy — and raises a string of unresolved dilemmas (teiku) about consecrating a body part, a valuation, or a field specifically 'for the altar.' A new mishna then rules that a child less than a month old cannot be valuated at all, since the Torah fixes no sum for him, launching a debate over what such a vow really means. The daf closes with a fresh mishna: is a gentile valuated, does he vow, both, or neither? Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda take mirror-image positions, and the Gemara probes where a gentile's Temple donation actually goes.

slides.title: 🦵 'The Leg of This Animal Is a Burnt Offering'
slides.subtitle: How much of the animal actually becomes sacred?

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: Only the leg becomes sacred — 'of it that one gives to the Lord, it shall be sacred,' not all of it. Sell the animal for its burnt-offering value; the proceeds are non-sacred except for that limb's share.

lines.speaker: Sages
lines.text: No — the extra word 'shall be' includes the WHOLE animal. Naming even one limb sanctifies the entire creature.

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: I agree only with a vital exception: if the limb named is one the animal's LIFE depends on — its head — then I too say the whole animal becomes holy.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: But Rava, you yourself ruled that consecrating a male animal 'for its value' still gives it inherent sanctity! Doesn't that collapse your distinction?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Only when the WHOLE animal is named 'for its value.' Naming just one limb 'for its value' — as with the head — is an entirely different case.

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Does naming one part of a body or one part of its value pull the rest along with it? The Gemara finds the answer depends on exactly what was named and for what purpose.

slides.title: ❓ Three Dilemmas for the Altar — All Left Standing
slides.subtitle: When something is consecrated specifically for the altar (מִזְבֵּחַ) rather than ordinary Temple upkeep
rows: 'The value of my head — for the altar'
Judged by the head's dignity (whole self) vs. only the head, since we've never seen a non-offering-eligible item judged by dignity
Reduced for a poor person like ordinary valuations, vs. paid in full since altar items are always redeemed at full value
Redeemed at the Torah's fixed rate (50 shekel per kor of barley seed) vs. market value

slides.title: 👶 Valuating a Child Under a Month — What Did He Really Mean?
slides.subtitle: The Torah fixes no erech for an infant less than one month old

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna: a baby under a month is not valuated — no erech applies. What if someone vows his erech anyway?

columns.label: Rabbi Meir
columns.content: He must pay the baby's market value (damim). 'A person does not make his words for naught' — knowing there's no erech, he must have meant assessment

columns.label: The Rabbis
columns.content: He owes nothing — a person's words CAN be for naught. His statement is taken literally, and erech has no application here

nodes.content: 💡 The same Rabbi Meir logic extends further: one who vows 'the erech of this utensil,' or who consecrates ANOTHER person's animal, likewise must pay its value — since those declarations, too, cannot mean what they literally say

slides.title: ⚖️ Three Near-Identical Cases, Each Needing Its Own Teaching
slides.subtitle: Why didn't Rav simply derive one ruling from another?

boxes.title: A Utensil ('erech keli alai')
items: No possibility of error — everyone knows utensils have no erech
So he clearly meant damim (market value)

boxes.title: Another's Animal
items: He cannot consecrate what isn't his, but an animal CAN in principle be consecrated
Rav: he still meant damim, intending to buy it first and then offer it

boxes.title: A Child Under a Month
items: Here one COULD mistakenly believe erech applies, since it does for a one-month-old child
Rabbi Meir needed a separate ruling to block that specific error

slides.title: 🌍 Can a Gentile Vow — or Be Valuated?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's mirror-image dispute, and its aftermath

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: Rabbi Meir — a gentile IS valuated (if a Jew vows his value) but does NOT vow; Rabbi Yehuda — the reverse: he vows, but is not valuated. Both agree he can vow another's assessment and be the object of an assessment vow

2️⃣ Rabbi Meir's proof: 'the children of Israel' excludes gentiles from vowing; 'a man' re-includes them for being valuated, since the verse 'includes more' there — like a deaf-mute or minor, who ARE valuated but cannot vow
3️⃣ Rabbi Yehuda's proof runs the reverse comparison: the verse includes more in the vowing category — like a tumtum, who DOES vow but is not valuated

4️⃣ Rava's verdict: Rabbi Meir's HALAKHA is sound (Ezra 4:3, 'you have nothing to do with us to build our Temple') but his PROOF is weak; Rabbi Yehuda's PROOF is sound, but his HALAKHA seems to contradict that same verse

callout.label: Where does the money go?
callout.text: Rav Ḥisda/Avimi: a gentile's valuation is interred, unused. But a baraita imposes me'ilah liability on gentile Temple-upkeep consecrations — so Rava resolves that Rabbi Yehuda actually holds the money IS used for upkeep, and Ezra's rejection of the gentiles was about weakening the builders' hands, not a halakhic exclusion.

summary.principle: Naming a single part of a body, a value, or a person pulls in the rest only under specific conditions the Gemara works out case by case — whether a limb is vital, whether the consecration targets the altar, whether a declaration could plausibly mean what it literally says, and whether the declarant is a Jew or a gentile.

flowSteps.content: 🦵 'Leg is a burnt offering': R' Meir — only the limb; Sages — the whole animal (unless R' Meir's own vital-organ exception applies)
❓ Consecrating 'for the altar' — head, valuation, or field — three separate dilemmas, all left as teiku

columns.content: 👶 Child under a month: R' Meir says pay damim ('words aren't for naught'); Rabbis say nothing owed
🌍 Gentile: R' Meir — valuated, doesn't vow; R' Yehuda — vows, isn't valuated; both agree on assessment vows

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a vow's precise wording, target, and context each shape exactly how far its consecration reaches

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Meir, if one says 'the leg of this animal is a burnt offering,' what becomes sacred?
o: The entire animal
Only the leg — the animal is sold for burnt-offering use, with proceeds non-sacred except for that limb's value
Nothing at all, since the declaration is invalid
Only if the leg happens to be a vital organ
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir derives from 'of it that one gives...it shall be sacred' that only the specified part becomes sacred, not the whole animal — unless the named part is one the animal's life depends on.

quiz.q: What is the outcome of the three dilemmas about consecrating a head's value, one's valuation, or a field specifically 'for the altar'?
o: All three are resolved in favor of full inclusion of the whole item
All three are resolved in favor of exclusion
All three are left unresolved as teiku
The Gemara rejects all three questions as illegitimate
quiz.e: Rabba's, Rava's, and Rav Ashi's dilemmas each end with the Gemara's formula 'teiku' — the question stands unresolved.

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Meir rule that one who vows the valuation ('erech') of a child less than a month old must pay the child's market value?
o: Because Jewish courts impose a monetary penalty for meaningless vows
Because 'a person does not make his words for naught' — knowing there is no erech for such a child, he must have intended its assessment (damim)
Because the Torah explicitly fixes a market-value sum for infants
Because such a vow is treated as a false oath requiring atonement
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir's principle is that a person's statement is never meaningless; since he knew erech doesn't apply, his true intent must have been damim.

quiz.q: Why did Rav need to teach separately that one who vows the 'erech' of a utensil, and one who vows the 'erech' of a child under a month, both owe damim, rather than deriving one ruling from the other?
o: Because a utensil and a child are governed by completely unrelated Torah verses

Because with a utensil there's no room for genuine error at all, while with the child one could mistakenly believe erech applies (as it does for a one-month-old), so each situation needed its own ruling
Because Rabbi Meir disagreed with himself between the two cases
Because only the child case involves the Temple treasury
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that the utensil case has no possibility of error, while the child's case does (since erech applies to a slightly older child) — so the identical conclusion had to be taught twice, for two different reasons.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what do Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda agree about regarding a gentile, despite their opposite rulings on erech?
o: A gentile is excluded from every Temple-related law
A gentile can vow to donate another's assessment (damim) and can himself be the object of such an assessment vow
A gentile can never contribute anything to the Temple treasury
A gentile is treated identically to a minor in every respect
quiz.e: The mishna states that both tannaim agree gentiles vow to donate another's assessment and are the object of such vows — their dispute is limited to erech (valuation).
